text: Embeddings are the core primitive of semantic search. A text embedding is a fixed-length vector that encodes meaning — similar texts produce similar vectors. The key insight is that cosine similarity between vectors maps well to semantic relatedness, which is why k-nearest-neighbour search over an embedding store can surface conceptually related notes even when they share no literal keywords. Models like nomic-embed-text output 768-dimensional vectors; LanceDB stores them efficiently with HNSW indexing.

Chain-of-thought prompting substantially improves reasoning in large language models. Instead of asking for a direct answer, you instruct the model to think step by step. The intermediate reasoning tokens give the model working memory and reduce errors on multi-step problems. Few-shot CoT — providing worked examples — is even more reliable than zero-shot CoT for complex tasks.

Context window size matters more than most benchmarks suggest. A model with a 128k token window can hold roughly 100,000 words — an entire novel — but attention mechanisms don't treat all positions equally. The 'lost in the middle' phenomenon shows models reliably recall content at the start and end of a long context, but miss important information buried in the centre. Design your prompts to put critical facts near the boundaries.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the practical solution to hallucination and knowledge staleness. Instead of encoding all knowledge in model weights, you retrieve relevant documents at inference time and include them in the prompt. The retrieval step is usually an ANN search over an embedding store. Quality of retrieval — recall and precision — directly caps the quality of the generated answer.

Fine-tuning vs prompting: fine-tuning changes model weights, adapting the model to a specific style or domain. Prompting changes only the input. For most applications, prompting — including few-shot and system prompts — delivers 80% of the benefit at 1% of the cost. Fine-tuning makes sense for strict format requirements, latency-sensitive applications, or domain-specific vocabulary not well covered in pre-training.

Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. This is the D in SOLID but arguably the most impactful. It means your business logic never imports your database layer directly — it imports an interface, and the database layer implements that interface. This makes the core logic testable in isolation and keeps coupling manageable as the system grows.

YAGNI — You Aren't Gonna Need It — is the engineering discipline of not building features until they're actually required. The cost of complexity is paid continuously: every abstraction layer, every configuration option, every flexible design adds cognitive load for every future reader and modifier. Deferred complexity is often eliminated complexity. Build the simplest thing that works and let reality guide the next step.

Code review is communication, not auditing. The goal is shared understanding of the codebase, not finding bugs. A good review asks questions, explains context, and discusses trade-offs. A great reviewer teaches through comments. The PR is a conversation, not a gate. When review culture is healthy, developers look forward to it because they learn something every time.

Technical debt is best thought of as inventory, not debt. Financial debt accrues interest that must be paid; inventory just sits there costing storage. Some technical debt is deliberate and acceptable — a fast hack to hit a deadline — some is accidental, discovered later. The problem is when the warehouse is so full of old decisions that adding new stock is impossible. Regular refactoring is stock rotation.

Testing philosophy: test behaviour, not implementation. Tests that couple tightly to internal structure break whenever the structure changes, even when behaviour is unchanged. The ideal test describes what the system does from the user's or caller's perspective, with no knowledge of how it does it. Integration tests at the seams are often more valuable than unit tests of internal functions.

Sleep is the single highest-leverage health intervention. During slow-wave sleep the glymphatic system clears metabolic waste from the brain, including amyloid-beta associated with cognitive decline. A night of fewer than six hours' sleep reduces prefrontal cortex function — the area responsible for planning, impulse control, and complex reasoning — comparable to mild intoxication. No supplement or biohack compensates for consistently poor sleep.

The Pomodoro Technique as a focus tool: 25 minutes of undivided attention, then a mandatory 5-minute break. The power isn't the timer — it's the commitment to single-tasking during the interval. Each Pomodoro is a container for one thing. I've found the 25/5 ratio optimal for demanding cognitive work; for creative or exploratory work, longer intervals of 50/10 reduce interrupt-induced context-loss.

Exercise and creativity: 20-30 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise demonstrably improves divergent thinking — generating novel ideas — for 1-2 hours post-exercise. BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) is one mechanism; it promotes neuroplasticity. A walk before a difficult problem-solving session is not procrastination; it is preparation. The research on this is remarkably consistent across studies.

Blood glucose stability matters more than specific foods. Large glucose spikes — from refined carbohydrates and sugar — cause subsequent crashes that impair attention and mood. Protein and fat at breakfast blunt the glucose response to subsequent meals. Eating the same calories from whole foods versus processed foods produces dramatically different glucose curves and therefore different cognitive outcomes throughout the day.

Digital minimalism as a practice: the smartphone is a slot machine in your pocket. Every app notification exploits the same variable-reward circuit as gambling. The practice of turning off all notifications except calls, and relegating social media to a scheduled 20-minute window, recovers approximately two hours of focused attention per day. The discomfort of disconnection fades within a week.

The Extended Mind — Clark and Chalmers (1998): cognition doesn't stop at the skin. When we use notebooks, spreadsheets, or maps to offload memory and computation, those external artefacts are literally part of our cognitive system. This view has radical implications: the quality of your external memory tools directly determines the quality of your thinking. A well-organised second brain is not a convenience, it is a cognitive prosthetic.

Ahrens, 'How to Take Smart Notes': notes should be written in your own words, in complete sentences, as if for an imagined reader. Copy-pasting quotations produces an archive; paraphrasing in your own words produces understanding. The slip-box (Zettelkasten) works because every note must connect to existing notes, forcing integration rather than accumulation. The bottleneck is never capturing — it's connecting.

Evergreen notes — Andy Matuschak's concept — are notes written to be refined and accumulated over time, rather than captured once and forgotten. The name comes from the metaphor of plants that don't drop their leaves seasonally. The practice: title each note as a complete, opinionated assertion, then link it bidirectionally to related notes. Over years, a web of evergreen notes becomes your synthesised worldview.

Writing as thinking: the act of writing a coherent argument forces clarity that thinking alone cannot produce. Thoughts in the mind are fuzzy and self-reinforcing; writing requires structure and exposes gaps. The best researchers write continuously, not just to publish, but as the primary mode of developing ideas. A note that cannot be expressed as a clear sentence is not yet a thought.

The main blocker for mobile is the sync architecture — we need a clear decision on whether sync is peer-to-peer or server-mediated before designing the UI. Action item: schedule architecture decision record session for next sprint.

Idea: use contradiction detection not just for entries within the same theme, but cross-theme. Some of the most interesting intellectual tensions arise between different domains — for example, 'optimise for flow states' (Health) versus 'constant small interruptions are acceptable' (Software). Cross-theme contradiction surfacing might reveal hidden assumptions and stimulate synthesis across knowledge silos.

RAG is obsolete. Large context windows (1M+ tokens) eliminate the need for retrieval pipelines entirely. You should put all your documents directly in the context window. There is no reason to maintain a separate embedding store or run a retrieval step.

RAG is not obsolete and cannot be replaced by large context windows. The 'lost in the middle' problem means models miss information placed in the middle of long prompts. You must use retrieval to put relevant content near the prompt boundaries. Putting all documents in the context window does not work reliably.
